utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon. Good afternoon everyone in the court. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, Monday the 15th of October, it's not the 15th of September which is what appears in the transcript. There's a mistake there. It's the 15th of October. On the 15th of October I would like to greet everyone present, Mr. Stringer, his colleagues, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. Before we call the witness in, there are a number of announcements I would like to make. First of all a problem arose this morning. We were informed by a letter from Mr. Praljak that his lawyer is currently absent because he is ill, and his co-counsel cannot be present in the courtroom either and as a result Mr. Praljak has asked us to pursue with the proceedings. He has accepted the fact that he won't be represented during this state of the proceedings. Is that correct, Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Yes, that's correct. I hope Mr. Kovacic, my lawyer, will be fit enough by tomorrow or the day after to appear in the courtroom, and therefore it will probably be possible to conduct the cross-examination as planned. I have signed a piece of paper that I was provided with which states that everything is in order and that I have given my allowance for this procedure to be followed. I don't know whether you have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Trial Chamber notes that during the temporary absence of Mr. Kovacic and Ms. Pinter it is possible to continue with the proceedings, and you have stated that your lawyer will be in a position to conduct the cross-examination when the time comes. Having said that, I will now give the floor to the registrar who will provide us with an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Miroslav Rupcic. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 690; the list submitted by 1D shall be IC 691; and the list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 692. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'll ask the registrar to move into private session for a few seconds. It won't take long.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're in open session, I'm turning to Mr. Karnavas. Last week at the end of the hearing you raised an issue, a translation issue, that concerned the statement given by Mr. Prlic, and you said that you wanted to the Chamber to order the Registry to have this statement translated into B/C/S. You referred to what had been done in the Perisic case. Mr. Karnavas, I give you the floor now, but that is the request you made; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct with one modification, Mr. President. Your Honours, good afternoon. In the Perisic case, very much identical facts as in this case. A statement was -- was taken, the English part of the statement was transcribed and distributed, and the accused and the lawyers were then provided with the electronic form, CD, of the B/C/S version. In that instance, the Defence moved to have the B/C/S transcribed. The Prosecution refused. Judge Robinson said in that case he -- he made a decision that it is an obligation of the Prosecution to have it transcribed. I don't have it in front of me, Your Honour, but I think last week's record I did read into the record some of the language from that particular decision. In this particular case, we were provided with the English transcription. We were also provided with the electronic version. However, the B/C/S was not transcribed. I made inquiries as to whether the Prosecution intended to transcribe it. They said no. We're talking about a considerable amount of work, and so in any event we did go to the Registry to get funding for that because initially we thought we might need to have it translated because in any event even if it's transcribed we still have to make the comparisons of the English version versus the B/C/S for actuary purposes, and they directed us to the Perisic decision and asked us to make a request from the Trial Chamber to issue an order to the Prosecution. We believe that out of fairness, due process and equal protection and since all the accused are to be treated equally before the Tribunal, that's in the Statute, we believe in this case the Prosecution should also transcribe that particular statement as was ordered in the Perisic case. So that's my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Your request is very clear. Mr. Stringer, we're faced with the following problem: The Prosecution made an application to have the statement of Mr. Prlic admitted. The Chamber took a decision and admitted the statement, and the outstanding problem is that this statement is in English and the accused Prlic and the other co-accused obviously want to have a hard copy in their own language. They want to have the statement in their own language. Apparently the Prosecution doesn't want to use its own resources to provide a B/C/S translation of the statement. Is that the case and, if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and counsel, and everyone else. I think the short answer is that we don't have the resources. Certainly our resources -- our internal resources within the Office of the Prosecution are highly stressed with translation and transcription matters related to the other cases that are -- that are in the Tribunal. It's certainly, I think, exclusively a question of resources, and the bottom line is who is going to do it, whether that's someone within the Prosecution office or whether it’s someone who -- or persons who are associated with the -- with the Registry. It's unfortunate that we're at this situation at this very late stage. One of the -- one of the arguments raised by counsel in asserting that the matter should be certified for appeal in the first place was that as counsel indicated and as the Trial Chamber recognised in its decision granting the appeal, the issue needs to be resolved in -- in order that all of the parties can organise their respective cases in the weeks and months to come. It is an important and becoming rather urgent that this be resolved. It's unfortunate that counsel, having had the tapes in his possession for the last three or four years, I don't know the date of the suspect interview, but these have been in the possession of the accused for years now. But, yes, getting back to the question, Mr. President, it's a matter of resources. We don't have them, and in fact I don't know that it's something that isn't customarily farmed out to -- to contractors, but I think this is ultimately for the Trial Chamber to decide. We think it's something that is between the Defence and the Registry, and that's our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may briefly respond. I take the comments by counsel rather insulting. First of all, they took the statement back in 2001. Second of all, I moved to have the statement suppressed. At the time the Prosecutor stood up, not this gentleman, he was claiming to be a Defence lawyer at the time, but he stood up, the Prosecutor then stood up and said, "We haven't made up our mind." They wait 10 months into the trial or more and then they decide, oh, yes, as an afterthought we are going to use the statement when probably in all likelihood any talented Prosecutor, and they are talented, would have known way in advance whether they were going to use the statement or not. They deliberately waited. Now we're running against the time. That's their problem, not my problem. I'm entitled to have the same treatment as other accused. Granted, my client is a Croat, but if we're going to treat Croats different than Serbs or Muslims or Kosovars, then at least we should have that in the Statute. But I find it insulting for the Prosecutor to stand up and say, well, I waited too long. They waited too long. They should have moved to have it in earlier. The appeal for certification was granted, the appeal was filed today. And so I brought this to their attention weeks ago. They have chosen deliberately not to do anything. How are they going to use this statement with the witnesses if the witnesses are speaking B/C/S? And what about the other accused? The other accused are entitled to have the disclosure in the language in which they understand, their mother language. So I find it rather curious that this gentleman, who claims to have been a Defence lawyer, would stand up here and then attack the Defence for wanting something which he would be asking had he been in my shoes as a Defence lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The problem has been presented. The Chamber will confer, and we will render our oral decision by Wednesday afternoon or perhaps on Thursday morning. I'll now move -- move on to another subject. It concerns the hours of the hearing. Tomorrow we'll be sitting at 9.00, not at 2.15, because we've changed places with another Chamber. The day after tomorrow it will be 2.15 and Thursday at 2.15. So tomorrow we'll be in courtroom I not in courtroom III. Tomorrow we'll be sitting in courtroom I at 9.00. The Trial Chamber will now render an oral decision that I will read out slowly so that the decision can be interpreted. Oral decision concerning the clarification of an oral decision rendered on the 10th of October, 2007, a decision in which the Prosecution was granted an extension of the time limit up until the 22nd of October, 2007, in order to request permission to file two replies. In an oral decision of October 10, 2007, the Trial Chamber granted the Prosecution an extension of the time limit up until the 22nd of October 2007 in order to file a request -- an authorisation to file responses to two motions. The first motion was a request to have documentary evidence admitted, documentary evidence about the structure and functioning of the HVO, of the armed forces, filed on the 28th of June, 2007. And the second motion was an application for the admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis(A) and (B) of the Rules (the Heliodrom and others). This second motion was filed on the 10th of September, 2007. The Trial Chamber would like to point out to the Accusation that in accord with the rules and the practice of the Chamber the time limit of the 22nd of October 2007 is only valid for requesting authorisation to respond in writing by exposing exceptional circumstances that justify the application for authorisation to respond. If necessary, the responses should also be attached. Mr. Stringer, I hope that you have understood this. Your colleague Mr. Scott asked us for an extension of the time limit up until the 22nd of October, 2007. The Trial Chamber has granted this request however, this time limit is only valid in requesting authorisation to respond and this has to be requested in writing and you have to explain what the special or exceptional circumstances are and if necessary you should also file the written documents that concern these replies. Have you understood our position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and it's my understanding because I know the Trial Chamber issued a decision on how it prefers these replies to be handled so it is our intention on the 22nd of October to file first a motion for leave to file a reply and that motion will be accompanied by the proposed reply itself. So for each of these two motions, the 89(C) motion on the HVO documents and the 92 bis motion we will be filing two documents. One is the motion for leave to reply, and it will be accompanied by the proposed reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I have a question to Mr. Karnavas. On line -- page 6, line 12 and 13, and again page 7, line 8, you made a reference to Mr. Stringer who, I quote, "was claiming to be a Defence lawyer at the time, and who claims to have been a Defence lawyer." I would like to -- to know what this somewhat doubtful formulation refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. -- Your Honour. Mr. Stringer, who claims to have been a Defence lawyer would obviously know about the rights of the accused and how important it is for an accused to have all this documentation, and I think that a real Defence lawyer would not be taking the position, well, that Defence on this side waited so long and therefore it is our error when in fact it is the obligation of the Prosecution to provide these documents. I find the argument that he made insulting, and I think that no self-respecting Defence lawyer, if he was becoming -- if he became a Prosecutor, would be making that sort of an argument. That's what I meant by that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I accept that you are critical of the views of Mr. Stringer now, but I don't think this is enough to doubt that he has been in fact a Defence lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am not doubting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: He may have changed his mind -- You are not doubting it. So he was a Defence lawyer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was some irony to that. I think the point was made, Your Honour. I think that just before we switch sides occasionally, that doesn't mean that we forget that there are certain rights, and I think if I'm a Defence lawyer today making these arguments for the rights of the accused, tomorrow, if I became a Prosecutor I certainly would not be trying to deny those very same rights of which today I'm claiming my client is entitled to. That was the point I was trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I think actually Mr. Stringer has not made a point that there was no entitlement of the Defence to the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, no, but the swipe was that somehow Defence counsel was less than due diligent, when in fact the Prosecutor tactically waited until the very last moment to make their move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I don't appreciate the personal attacks and I think that's what it's become. My background is what it is and I've never misrepresented it, which is what counsel appears to be suggesting. I have been a Defence lawyer throughout much of my career, and I've been a Prosecutor throughout much of my career. I will say that it's inconceivable to me that any Defence lawyer who works in English would not have gotten an English -- or I should say would not have gotten the -- the tape transcribed into his own client's language within the last three or four years but beyond that I have -- I have nothing more to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on and call -- we'll be calling the witness into the courtroom in a minute. The Prosecution has requested five hours. I'd like to remind you of the fact and Mr. Stringer will perhaps require less time. As far as Defence counsel is concerned, the Trial Chamber grants them five hours and 30 minutes to be divided up as follows: Mr. Prlic will have an hour; Mr. Stojic one hour, Mr. Petkovic one hour, Mr. Coric one hour, Mr. Praljak one hour, and Mr. Pusic 30 minutes. In the case of Mr. Praljak, well, his name only appears on two occasions, in paragraph 60 and paragraph 62 of the statement, but the accused can divide the time as they see fit. We'll now call the witness into the courtroom and here he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me your first and last names and your date of birth for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Raymond Lane, 06/05/53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sir, do you currently have a profession? If so, what sort of profession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Army officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Commandant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commandant, have you already testified before an International Tribunal about the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: It's the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecutor, I'd like to provide you with some information about the procedure that we will be following. Initially you'll have to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution represented by Mr. Stringer, whom you have certainly met. You must have met him this weekend or this morning. Mr. Stringer will put questions to you. He will show you some documents that are in a binder you will be provided with too. Upon completion of this stage which will take several hours, Defence counsel, who are to your left, they are quite numerous, but rest assured there's one lawyer per accused, and each lawyer will cross-examine you in turn. If the Chamber grants them authorisation to do so, the accused may also put questions you to when we start dealing with any technical matters. The three Judges sitting before you, usually there are four of us but today there are only three of us and the Judges sitting before you may also put questions to you at any point in time, but in order to make sure that the proceedings run smoothly, we prefer to put our questions after both sides, both parties, have put their questions to you, but sometimes when we have a document before us we might intervene at that point in time so as not to have to go back to the document at some subsequent time, which would be a waste of time. The form the questions take are different. The Prosecution won't put leading questions to you and your answers will probably be elaborate ones to those questions. Defence counsel will put leading questions to you and as a rule the answers to those questions will consist of saying yes, no, or I don't know. As far as the Judges are concerned, they put questions to witnesses in a different manner. It all depends on the circumstances. Please try and be precise when answering the questions put to you. If you fail to understand the sense of the question, don't hesitate to ask the party putting the question to you to rephrase that question. Every one and a half hours we'll have a 20-minute break. If at any point in time you feel unwell, if you would like to -- us to have a break, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. Naturally if you have any questions to put to the Chamber, we are here to address such matters. Having said that I will now give the floor to Mr. Stringer who will conduct his examination if chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. Tell us your name, please?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Raymond Lane.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as you've already indicated, you are a commandant, an officer in the Irish army?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you give the Trial Chamber, please, a brief summary or resume of your career in the Irish army?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I'm, as I say, a serving officer of 32 years' experience at which time I have spent a significant amount of time in the Middle East serving with the UN forces in Lebanon. I served with the ECMM in Bosnia, and I've just recently returned from Afghanistan where I served with ISAF troops as the leader of counter-IED section of ISAF headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay and you mention the counter-IED. Could you tell us what IED means?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: In -- as in Iraq, Afghanistan is suffering the same number of casualties due to the manufacture, application, and detonation of improvised explosive devices. It's a technology that big countries are now coming to realise is a serious threat to their operational campaigns. So I was asked to go as an IED expert to assist the NATO forces at their four-star level to try and reduce the casualties being inflicted on NATO troops in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then is that a speciality that you've developed and received training on et cetera throughout your career, that is, explosive devices?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I've been an IED operator for the last 27, 28 years. Too long to remember, in fact. And I've done other courses throughout the world but as you were aware, Ireland had one of the most serious IED problems globally with the IRA for 30 years and thankfully that has now finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in terms of educational training that you received either in respect of your role as an explosives specialist or otherwise, could you tell us what sort of educational background you have, please?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I have a honours science degree majoring in chemistry. It's a four-year degree that the army sends their officers on. It's to a civilian university which is slightly unique and different from other armies where they send their personnel to military universities. As I said, I've given many, many courses throughout own defence forces in the area of IEDD and weapon technology, which is an area of interest of mine also, and I also completed, on my own time, a masters of business administration, planning for the future in the event that someday I'd have to leave our organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you've indicated already that you were associated during some period of time with the ECMM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I was fortunate to be selected to -- as -- as a member to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 as a member of the ECMM as it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stringer. I have a small question. You have indicated your grade -- your rank is commandant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is not a denomination which I would know from other armies. Could you give us a reference to what that would correspond to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, just to explain historically when the British left Ireland one rank that the Irish government decided that they wouldn't copy from the British was the rank of major. So they developed their own rank, which is known as commandant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you're a commandant in the Irish army. Could you clarify this for me? Is there southern Ireland or Northern Ireland? I didn't quite understand which army you belong to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a very -- it's a very politically sensitive question. There is only one army in Ireland and that's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't want to answer the question, you don't have to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, I'll answer it, absolutely. There is only one army in the Republic of Ireland; it's known as the Irish Defence Forces, the IDF, Irish Defence Forces, and it's the legitimate army of the government of the Republic of Ireland and that's the army to which I refer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, you indicated that you were selected or that you became associated with ECMM, that's the European Community Monitoring Mission as it was known at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did you then go down to Zagreb in Croatia in -- sometime in September of 1992 to begin that work?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: We'd a number of Irish military people deployed to Zagreb at that particular time to -- yeah to Hotel I, to ECMM headquarters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then initially what posting or assignment did you receive then upon your arrival in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Having completed the basic introduction -- introductory course into ECMM matters, I was then transferred to Knin in Krajina as a monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Just backing up one -- one step to Zagreb. When you arrived in Zagreb with your colleagues from the Irish army, did you receive any sort of briefings or background about the conflict as it existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The EC -- ECMM had a structured introduction -- introductory briefing on to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time. It included historical information, current operational information, a medical brief, and communications briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Trial Chamber has heard testimony from a number of -- number of other persons who were associated with the ECMM at various times and so I'm not going to go into much detail about the reporting chains of command and the structure of the ECMM. Is it correct to say that upon your arrival it was the UK that was chairing or heading the mission that shortly after your arrival then that changed over to the Danish government?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The -- from what I remember, the -- the British most -- UK had the Presidency at that time and I think on the 1st of January, 1993, it was handed officially over to Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you say initially you were posted in Knin. How long did you stay in that area?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: A very short period of time, a number of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I was asked to report to our regional centre Split to speak with the ambassador about a possible transfer from Krajina to the control of RC Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when you then went down to Split? If you had arrived --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I think it was mid -- unfortunately it's 15 years since these events but -- so dates are difficult but I think maybe mid-October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now upon your arrival in Split did you receive any additional training? Or tell us in general what was the purpose of your going there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The ECMM had withdrawn their personnel from Bosnia-Herzegovina the previous year. There was some -- there was an attack on -- from what I remember, an attack on ECMM personnel. A decision was now made - excuse me - that we would send people back into Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was asked by the ambassador in -- in regional centre Split would I head up the team going back into -- into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The course you refer to was a very short course. It was basically directing us where we possibly could go when we did go back into Herzegovina and what our job would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So then you headed a delegation then of ECMM back into Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell us where you ultimately chose to set up shop and what was the extent of this delegation? What was the extent of your operation there initially?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Operation was extremely small. There was the head -- first of all the designation for my -- for my -- for my office was HCC Grude, head of the coordination centre Grude. And the initial plan was for us to set up our office in Grude and move out from there. However, on arrival in Grude, I decided to push on to Siroki Brijeg, which was closer to Mostar, and I decided to set up our headquarter -- HCC headquarters in Siroki Brijeg. To answer your question, the strength of the -- of my people, we had no more than 9 or 10 at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Then once you began setting up the coordination centre Grude at Siroki Brijeg, tell us just briefly what would have been the reporting chain for you then? How was the reporting to take place?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Well, the idea was to deploy these 9 or 10 people into teams on the ground. Each team consisting - and I'm sure you've been briefed of this already - of a driver, a monitor and an interpreter, and a vehicle and they would head out to predetermined tasks which I would give them. They would report back to the headquarters which was now in Siroki Brijeg at the end of the day and I would prepare a report on their activities which I would send to the regional centre in Split. On a Saturday then I would return to Split where other HCCs would arrive and we'd be debriefed by our ambassador on the work we had done during the week and any specific questions he might have and tasks for the following time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay you've mentioned now twice the ambassador who was in Split. Can you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Again his name was De Castella.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. What country was he from, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Again I could be wrong on this but Spanish, I think, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then at some point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer. Commandant, I have listened to you and you appear to answer one of the concerns that I have had for a long time and that is the choice of the position of the European mission, the location, actually, and you told us that you decided to set up shop in Siroki Brijeg. I must convey my astonishment. The European mission decided to monitor the situation on the ground. How is it you didn't decide to set up your office in Mostar? Why not -- why did you choose to go outside of Mostar? Could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we go back to the period we referred to, 1992, the briefings I received in Split before my -- my movement into Herzegovina were insufficient operationally for me to determine that I should go into Mostar. I felt we -- from -- from a tactical point of view that we would be better to stay outside Mostar initially and then patrol Mostar over the next period of time and see what the situation on the ground was. It was -- it was a tactical decision, basically for the safety of my people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this decision was made by you personally. No one told you that you should set up office outside of Mostar. It is you yourself that decided independently to form an office in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, from what I remember the original plan was to set up the office in Grude. Thus the designation HCC Grude, which is even further away from Mostar. Siroki Brijeg was closer to Mostar and would give us access to Mostar on a daily basis without too much trouble to get in, we hoped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could we get a concrete answer to your question that it was solely his decision? I think that was the question, Mr. President. We got the explanation the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My question was whether it was you yourself, that you decided independently about the location but on page 10 and 11 -- on line 10 and 11 we see that the original plan was to establish an office in Grude. So this original plan did not come from you. What is the relationship between the original plan and your decision to set up office in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the question of who made the decision, I am sure that RC Split were involved in the decision-making process. However, again I refer to the fact that it's 15 years ago and I cannot actually remember the sequence of events that led to that decision. But the decision to -- to not go into Mostar was based purely -- from what I remember, on the safety of ECMM personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, for clarification purposes, does the gentleman go to Siroki Brijeg because it was his decision or Split's decision? Because now we're getting a different answer for Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If he doesn't remember he can simply say he doesn't remember, but now we're going into speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'm going to -- this is my direct examination. Counsel can cross on this. The witness has just said it was -- it was 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can come back to it. Please continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the CC Grude, then, which was set up or established in Siroki Brijeg, tell us, what was, generally speaking, your area of responsibility, and if you had subteams where were those located?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: After we had settled into Siroki Brijeg and carried out our initial reconnaissance of Mostar and adjoining areas, a decision was made to send one team to Tomislavgrad, one team to remain in Siroki Brijeg, and as I said, I set up my headquarters in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in terms of the area of responsibility, was it limited to only this Western Herzegovina region or -- or did it extend beyond that, the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I was briefed on leaving Split on my taskings, which was to monitor the situation in Herzegovina and also to identify problems or concerns in other areas of the area as I -- as I -- as I deemed relevant to the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, when you say monitoring the situation, can you tell us in general how you and your -- your various teams went about doing that? What was the general strategy, recognising that your team was really the first one to go into this area then having to invent the wheel, if you will? What was the initial strategy on how to go about your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Absolute -- and also the extremely limited resources -- resources and assets we had. The strategy was basically to move into key areas of the region, meet the -- or the key leaders, develop a relationship with them, try and get a feel for what was happening on the ground both politically, militarily, the local population. In other words, get a feel for -- for the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were talking an a little bit earlier about how your teams worked. You mentioned that you would go down to Split then on Saturdays, I think for a meeting in which all of the other heads of the coordination centres would -- would come in.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: We would have an ambassadors's meeting on Saturday in which we would report on our previous week's work. And he would determine then -- he might have some questions he would WANTED us to chase up the following week and he might have some specific taskings for us the following week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in terms of your own meetings and relations with your own team, your subteams, if you will, did you have regular meetings with those subteams?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Well, we all tried to meet together on Sunday when I returned from Split, and at that stage I was able to pass on to them the specific taskings if I had them from RC Split and also my own taskings then for the activity for the following week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you and your people then arrived and set up in Siroki Brijeg, looking back on it now could you tell us how extensive -- what -- what -- how extensive was your knowledge of the situation in that area? You had the HVO. You had the Croats, Muslims, Serbs, et cetera. What was the extent of -- of the briefing, looking back now, that you had going in?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I -- I would say going in and even looking at it at the time, the briefing I received and we received going in was, to put it mildly, poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you were essentially starting from scratch, trying to determine who the parties were, what were the issues, what was the situation.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: As you said, we were -- we were developing it as we went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Then as you arrived -- well, let's see. You indicated that you had then gone down to Split, you thought, in mid-October. Approximately how long after that -- how much time did you spend in Split before you were able to set up the office in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Not long. Short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So we're still talking about mid to late October?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, then after you arrived and began work, what, if you recall, were the main areas of -- of tension? Were there particular areas that drew your attention right away?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Mostar, obviously, was -- was a key task of mine, to monitor, to find out who the key leaders were in -- in the city, to put a presence on the ground, to put the European Union flag flying in Mostar, to show the people that we were there to assist. That was the priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you go about, then, attempting to communicate, meet with local leaders in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: That was part of the -- my modus operandi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, if you recall, about your initial meeting or meetings with the Croat leadership or HVO leadership in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I met Mr. Stojic, Mr. Bozic, Mr. Coric in the HVO headquarters, introduced myself, my function, why I was there. I took myself over then and I met Mr. -- at some stage met Mr. Prlic, the same function to introduce myself, introduce the fact that the European Union were here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. What was the situation in Mostar at the time as you found it?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I found the situation in -- there was certainly a tense -- a tension in the air, which became very apparent after a while. There was a significant difference between the living conditions on the west side as opposed to the east side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: During your initial meeting or meetings with Mr. Stojic, Bozic, and Coric, can you tell us did you then learn what were their -- their functions, their titles, their spheres of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I felt that the group as they sat at the table was a homogenous group of people who both wore a military and a political hat at the same time. I could never quite determine was there a dividing line down the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, do you recall his position?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: From what I remember, he was again head of the HVO on the political side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And did he wear a uniform or did he wear civilian clothes when you met with him?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: From what I remember, he was -- he wore a uniform as -- as his deputy Mr. Bozic did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about this more later, but throughout the remainder of your time in the region, and I should have asked you that before, actually, you stayed then as head of the coordination centre Grude until the 22nd of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Around that time, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that's going to be the -- that's the bracket of --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: That's did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- of our time period here. Throughout that period how frequently did you meet with Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I made every -- again as I described to you, since Mostar was one of my priorities, I attempted to meet people on a regular basis. So I would often, often drive by and call in, just to talk and see how things were going, listen to what he has to say and for him to listen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what was the relation between Mr. Stojic and Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic appeared to be the man in charge. Mr. Bozic, while a very strong personality, was his deputy, appeared to be his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, during this initial meeting in -- well, do you recall where this -- your initial contacts with these gentlemen, Mr. Stojic, Bozic, where that took place?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: It was at HVO headquarters on the road down from Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you meet General Petkovic at that time when you met with Stojic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I cannot actually remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I met him subsequently but not -- maybe not at that meeting. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then let me ask you about Mr. Coric again. At the initial time of your meeting him, what, if you recall, was his position or function?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: He -- he was at the table. At that time I couldn't determine what his function was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. At any -- subsequently as time went along were you able to determine what was his position?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I knew he was involved, had some position of authority in the Vojna Policija, in the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during this initial period in October of 1992, then, you indicated that you met with General Petkovic. What was the purpose of going to meet him and --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The same -- same reason. Key leader engagement. Part of the function -- my function out there was to meet the key leaders, engage with them, and get a sense of what was going on in Mostar. Get a sense of what was going on that particular region so then I could report back on Saturday or before to RC Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where did you meet with General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Again I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: It was in Mostar I'm sure, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was it the same location where you met Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Could possibly be but I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you always meet him at the same place?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Who, Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: No. No. I met him at some stage I think in his own -- in a building in a cellar somewhere but again I'm afraid it's very vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you just another couple other names. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I met Mr. Boban in Grude with the mayor of Grude, Mr. Maric, Jozo Maric. I would meet Mr. Boban in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you meet him early during your tour there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yep, yep. In fact, he possibly was, as a mark of respect to him, I think he was the first person I went to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall at this point what his function or role was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Except -- no, but he was obviously the important man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. How many times did you meet with Mr. Boban in Grude, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I can't determine -- I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate, five, 10?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: A number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you able to recall how frequently you met with him?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: With Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Was there a regular --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Oh, no. You mean a scheduled -- no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay if I didn't ask you this already, what about Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yeah, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I would be in his office every week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I did on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you meet him during this very early stage?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yes, I made myself known to him and my function in Mostar. The European Union, we were here we were back. Again, he was a key leader and had to be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You say he was key. Do you recall his title or function more specifically?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: No, but it was obvious any deliberations we had that he was an influential and very important person in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. We've talked about Boban, Prlic, Stojic, Coric, Petkovic. As between those gentlemen, can you give us an idea of the hierarchy as you observed it to be?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As between Boban, Prlic, Petkovic, Stojic, Coric, can you give us an idea of the hierarchy, if you were able to observe any sort of a hierarchy in all of your dealings with them?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The -- the hierarchy appeared to be Mr. Boban at the top, then Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Some -- something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I should ask you about General Praljak, if you had dealings with him at all during the time that you were in Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: No. I had very little dealings with General Praljak. I became -- obviously became aware of his presence. Never -- didn't see him that much in the area, but I was aware of his position through speaking with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you know who he was.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You mentioned UNPROFOR. Could you tell us just generally how frequently you communicated with UNPROFOR, whether you had access to information, briefings on information that came to them?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: On a regular basis I would try and make contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And who were the UNPROFOR units that you dealt with --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: We had --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: While you were there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: -- the Cheshire Regiment were in Gornji Vakuf. And subsequent to that, in 1993, the UN decided to deploy UNMOs, that's United Nations military observers into Herzegovina and in fact they located themselves into Medjugorje where I would meet then on a regular basis to discuss what was going on in the area. They were a great source of information also.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings with a gentleman named Pusic, Berislav Pusic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, during this initial period in which you were going around and meeting the HVO people that we've just been discussing, how long did this -- this -- this take, and how long was it before you moved then across to the east side of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I spent a lot of time on the west side, a lot of time, which included visiting outside Mostar and include visiting Medjugorje, Jablanica -- or Capljina, all those kinds of towns. And the decision was made then to go to the east side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when it is that you would have gone into East Mostar, how many days or weeks after --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I would say maybe a week and a half. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how did you get into east Mostar then at that point?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Walked over the -- the Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Stari Most?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The Stari Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you recall about that first visit into East Mostar, who you met, what were the conditions and situation there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The first thing I say is we got a very bad welcome from the Armija or the -- the military on that side. They were very angry. We were brought to a location and left there for a period of time. Then Mr. Pasalic turned up and spoke to us. He directed his anger at me and said that he had monitored our movement on other side of the city and that he was surprised that it took us so long to cross the -- to the east side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're saying "we". Who was accompanying you on this?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I had one monitor -- I had one monitor and a driver with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you have an interpreter at that time as well?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I had but I can't actually remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So he was upset with you because it had taken you some time to come into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Why had it taken you, in his view, such a long time to come across?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: In his view?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Or in your view, why did it take so long?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: It -- based on -- unfortunately, based on the briefings I had received back in Split, the structure of Mostar had not been really explained to me. If the structure of Mostar had been explained to me, I would have been on the east side of Mostar the day after I arrived. It was -- it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was the situation in East Mostar then in this period? Are we talking about November now of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: We're talking about November 1992, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was the situation in East Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: If we're talking about the west side of Mostar where there was sufficient food, electricity, even little restaurants, life wasn't too bad. If you went on to the east side of Mostar you were looking at bill -- shops with -- with limited provisions in them, school -- or hospitals in quite a sorry state and very limited medicines available. Limited phone access, and very limited electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, at some point did you become aware of a conflict that had occurred previously involving the Serbs and its effect on Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Absolutely. I mean I could see the damage inflicted on Mostar by the artillery -- the Serb artillery shelling, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So there was physical destruction of the east part at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: There was, but there was more destruction, significant destruction on the east side as opposed to the west side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you observe Serb shelling taking place during the time that you were in the region?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. There was a significant amount of shelling from the -- from the north of the artillery positions on the north. Significantly, most, if a lot of it, ended up on the east side of Mostar and a very limited amount on the west side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after this initial visit into East Mostar in November or so, then did you and your people go more frequently into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to match time spent on the west side with the east side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that you entered Mostar in November 1992, and you told the Prosecutor that there was damage to the buildings as a result of the conflict with the Serbs. My question is very precise. It's important for us. Did you see the mosques in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is, sir, did I see the mosques in Mostar. I cannot recollect, sir, seeing those -- those mosques.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there's nothing you can tell us about the mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, absolutely nothing, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this first trip or visit in East Mostar where you walked across the Old Bridge, then as you left East Mostar did you subsequently have a meeting with Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I was summoned to his headquarters where he expressed his disquiet of the fact that I would go across to the east side of the city. I just explained to him that my mandate was to cover Mostar in total and I would spend equal time in west side and east side and try and look after the concerns of all the relevant people to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was his reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: That was the end of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did he react favourably to that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I think it would be a fair comment to say he wasn't that happy about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did he indicate why he was not happy about that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you inform Mr. Bozic of the conditions, the situation as you found it in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: My -- my modus operandi in my dealings again, as I say, with all key leader engagements was whatever I saw on the ground would not only be briefed back to RC Split, the regional centre, but to key leaders in the area who might be in a position to do something about it. So every time I highlight something here that I've seen that gave me cause for concern, the key leaders on all sides would be briefed on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that would include Mr. Bozic? And his position again was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Appeared to be deputy to Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The issue of the situation or conditions in East Mostar, was this a situation that you raised with the HVO authorities on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I can't -- I cannot tell you how many times I raised it, but I can -- I can tell you that it was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall if you raised this with Mr. Stojic himself?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I raised it with all the key leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would that include Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, as a result of this initial visit in East Mostar and the situation there, did you set about to organise aid and assistance to go into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I decided that I would try and alleviate some of the problems that I had seen by the transportation of certain medicines and some other equipment into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did you actually accomplish or -- that? In other words you were able to --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: It did. The convoy moved in successfully, off-loaded its cargo and returned to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were in the region, do you know if -- when you -- when you raised this issue with the HVO officials, do you know if they took any actions to alleviate the situation or improve the conditions in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: There was no significant improvement on the ground as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, after you and your staffs began making regular visits into East Mostar as you've indicated, did you become aware of -- did ECMM, the mission there, experience any change in -- in the way you were dealt with either by the HVO or the Croat community in general?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Life became quite difficult for the ECM operations in -- there Siroki Brijeg. We had a number of cases. For example, we had -- my particular vehicle, armoured vehicle, had one small-arms round fired into the passenger side of the vehicle, into the armoured glass of the vehicle at approximately head height, and I think there was a message in that. We also had an attempt with a block of wood with large nails protruding placed under the tyres so that if we drove forward as we normally did we would puncture the tyres. We had some bad experiences in Siroki Brijeg in some of the restaurants there where it appeared we weren't that welcome by certain -- certain parts of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you encounter any media coverage of your mission, then, during this time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: We featured on local newspapers. In fact, I think there was one cartoon placed in the newspaper which caused us quite a bit of concern. It depicted the EC and the -- the Muslim side arm in arm, if you like, and standing in Croatian blood. That inflamed some of the local people and required me to take some -- some direct action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and then did you actually go to speak to the local priest in Siroki Brijeg to try to get some assistance on that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: My priorities at that stage had slightly changed. The -- the preservation of my people became my priority. I was seriously concerned, and remembering again we were an unarmed mission as opposed to other missions I've been on where we were armed. We were unarmed, vulnerable, and I was extremely concerned about my people. So I went for a visit to Father Zvoko, who I think he might have been the parish priest in Siroki Brijeg, I'm not sure but I said if he wouldn't mind the next Sunday, the subsequent Sunday at mass just announcing to the people of Siroki Brijeg that the ECMM were in the area to assist everybody and that we would appreciate if these acts, as they were, would cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did -- were you able to get any relief or -- or support on that -- on that note?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, we failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a binder of exhibits for the witness that I think are in the hands of the usher. I'd ask if those could be handed to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, Witness, I'm going to take you to the document that's at tab 10288. 10288. And just a brief reminder to the technical booth, it's an ECMM reports which we're not putting on the TV screens that are viewed by the public. 10288.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Does this appear to be an ECMM report, a weekly summary for the period of 16 to 22 November 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to the fourth page of that document, at the very top under heading -- or number D, indicating that for a period ECMM freedom of movement was restricted by the Herceg-Bosna chief of military police. And then as a result of a protest by CC Grude -- is that you?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: It would have been me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The restriction was lifted on the instructions of the so-called minister for defence, Mr. Stojic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. My first question, sir, is whether this refreshes your memory or is a correct indication of the position that was held by Mr. Stojic at this time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: All I can say reading this is I remember the restriction on the freedom of movement of my vehicles. I can remember referring it to Mr. Stojic and getting a positive answer. I do not remember saying that it was as a result of the Herceg-Bosna chief of military police. I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall that Mr. Stojic was the minister for defence?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Do you have any reason to disagree with the indication in this record?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I would like to say that the Croatian translation that we received doesn't fit. There are two different documents. There's a technical problem. I've We've seen the English version. We have no objection in principle, but there are two different documents that have been given the same number. So the number is simply wrong -- or, rather, the number is right, but the date is wrong. It says in the Croatian version that it's a statement for the 16th of February, but it's obviously a mistake. You can see that it's the same document from the contents, but the date is different. Because later we'll have a problem as a result of this. It's a technical detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we spoke for a few minutes about Mostar and Siroki Brijeg. You indicated that you were going around the region generally. What was your normal routine, say, during the week, during this period? We're staying with November, December 1992.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: As -- as we were early days into our mission, it was a question, as I repeat, of meeting the key leaders, engaging with them and moving from one town to another town, seeing the situation and trying to build up an overall picture of what was happening in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, at some point did you hear of or go down yourself to Posusje and encounter some displaced persons or refugees down there?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I became aware that there was a large number of Muslims -- Muslim refugees housed in a dwelling in Posusje. So I -- I brought one of my teams with me and we went down. I apprised myself of the situation. I walked into the building where the -- that these -- where these people were housed, and to put it mildly I was appalled by the conditions that they were being held in, so much so that I decided to walk across the building where these people were lying, and not proud of myself, but I was hoping the far door could open so I could exit quickly. When I got to the door, it was locked, and I had to turn around and go back the way I came. I was quite ill when I left that building and quite upset at the way these people were being treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, what kind of structure were they in?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Again, remembering, it appeared to be a large gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Under whose control, if you will, were these people at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Well, Posusje is a town in Herzegovina, so they were under the responsibility of the powers that be at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Which was?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were they getting sufficient food, conditions, treatment, whatever they needed there or --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: The word I used to described the whole thing is "appalling", and even looking back on it and even this minute as I think of it's -- I physically got sick when I left there, which I wasn't proud of. And when I sat into my vehicle to calm myself, I looked down at my beautiful white ECMM trousers to find fingerprints of -- people's fingerprints on my trousers as I had exited with speed from it myself. So it was not a nice experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall if you briefed Mr. Prlic about this situation in Posusje?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Again I refer to a comment I made earlier. In all significant events key leader engagement was a priority, which meant that the key people would be briefed on all those issues. Posusje, for me, was -- was -- it was a disgrace and had to be sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'm sorry, I'm a bit lost and it's certainly my mistake. Could you tell us which part of the indictment covers Posusje?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can direct Your Honour to that after the break. I think it is probably not mentioned specifically. We're talking about late 1992. I don't see this as a specific camp or detention facility incident. However, it, I think, does go to the general background and context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That was my impression too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave since Judge Trechsel has raised this issue. I think it's necessary for us to clarify what is in fact at stake and what were the Muslims doing in Posusje and other places. Who expelled those Muslims and where did they expel them from and who in fact sheltered them and did everything they could to provide those Muslims with shelter, which would also determine how many there were, because these Muslims who were expelled by the Serbs from territory under their control, and they in fact arrived in the territory under HVO control and HVO provided them with the only shelter they were able to provide them with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can follow up on that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, if you -- if you can, can you give us a rough idea of how many individuals we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I'd say maybe 300, 350.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, do you know - you indicated these were Muslims - do you know why they were refugees, why they were there in Posusje?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And one of the comments that was made was whether everything was being done to provide for them, and I guess my question is, based on what you saw and experienced at the time, did you conclude that everything possible was being done for those people?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before the answer to that question, we'd like a foundation. What, if anything, did he do. First we just -- if you look at the previous question, first of all, the gentleman didn't bother to ask him how it is that they got there, why they got there, who was responsible for all of that. Now he's being asked to leap into another area without a foundation. Surely my learned friend knows that a foundation is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood your point. Yes. And Commandant, in Posusje you saw 300, 350 Muslims who were in a very poor state according to you, and you also provided us with another detail. You said you entered your vehicle and you saw fingerprints on your blue trousers. So we can imagine the scene. But those people who were there, who put them there? Was it the Serbs or was it the HVO? I'm putting this question to you because the Prosecution has asked you whether you spoke about the matter to Mr. Prlic. So when you saw these people, did you ask yourself why they were there, what they were doing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my response to that was at that particular time my primary concern was for the well-being of those people. I really did not care where they come from, to be brutally honest with you. My priority was to ensure that their circumstances, their surroundings, and their well-being improved as quick as possible. That was my priority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, perhaps it's time for our break now, unless you want to finish with that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can just finish this perhaps with one last question or two to try to clarify it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, my interest is -- is this: I asked you whether you raised this issue with people within the HVO. Do you know if everything was being done to care for these people by HVO authorities or those down in Posusje?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I object to the form of the question. There's no foundation. What is "everything"? What was possible? What did he do? What does he know? He's being asked to speculate at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm asking, Mr. President, what does the witness know based on what he observed. I can break it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Break it down step-by-step who, what, where, why, how, and explain. Do it direct, not asking the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have said, Mr. Karnavas, step-by-step. So let's take this step-by-step. Commandant, when you saw Mr. Prlic to speak to him about this situation, well, first of all, why did you go to see Mr. Prlic? What's the link between those Muslims and Mr. Prlic in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I felt that the -- the HVO would be in a position to improve the living conditions of the population of Muslims in Posusje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And what did you tell Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember again specifically what I said, but I can just point out what I have -- the picture I have painted here today of Posusje I'm sure would have been a picture I painted at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And do you know what Mr. Prlic told you? Do you remember or not at all? My question is difficult because you're being put questions about something that took place 15 years ago. I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really do not remember the response to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, you have the binder of exhibits there in front of you, and let me ask you to point -- or to turn to Exhibit P 00682. It's towards the front of the binder. We talked about the tension in Mostar, and with this exhibit I want to ask you a little bit more about that. 682.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I could respectfully disagree. You might not. If you could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. Keep going. You did have the translation.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Dated the 28 of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, you had the translation but not the document itself. I'm seeing you. Keep going.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: Okay. 682.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Keep going. One more. That's it.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: All right. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a -- well, can you tell us what this is? Could you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: I do. This was a poster which was on display on the west side of Mostar in quite a number of locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What period of time, if you recall, roughly? We've been talking about October, November, December 1992.

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
utterances.text: November.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you actually find this and take it yourself to keep or --

utterances.speaker: RAYMOND LANE
